highlights.text: a single core idea: moving straight ahead, head-on, without turning the head aside or veering
**al-ṣayd (game, quarry)** — derived, on his account, from the same idea: the animal goes past in a straight, unswerving course
aṭfaʾahā: he put the fire out.
"Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God puts it out" (Q 5:64)
A verse is also cited: "Among the house of Banū ʿAdī there was strife, and Ziyād put it out."
carrying the same idea as the root he treated just before it: going round, encircling
a ṭawq (an encircling band or collar)
to be able to bear something is, as it were, to have encompassed it
Al-bi'r (the entry's central noun) — a well
This grounds a hadith criticizing a wealthy man who "stored up no good"
Ibn Fāris treats b-d-ʿ as two separate roots.
God as Originator of the heavens and the earth
Citing Q 46:9, "Say: I am no bidʿ among the messengers," he glosses bidʿ as "I am not the first."
the opening/bursting-forth of a thing, releasing water
a split in a waterskin, stone, or ground from which water gushes forth
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-ʿAjjāj about a bucket splitting
whose core meaning is reaching or arriving at a thing
"I reached the place," i.e. arrived at it.
"when they reach their term (balaghna ajalahunna)."
aḥmaq bilgh / balgh describes a fool who, despite his foolishness, still reaches what he wants
Its core, literal sense is "to poke or prick something with something"
ghamaza bi-jafnihi means "he winked" - he made a sign with his eyelid.
a single sound root whose core sense is "the opposite of smallness" — greatness or largeness
كبير (kabīr), with the intensive forms كُبَار and كُبَّار ("very great")
كِبَر (kibar): old age, decrepitude.
كِبْر (kibr): greatness or pride
In the legal saying "clientage (walāʾ) belongs to the kubr," it means the most senior kinsman
The root has two separate core meanings.
"And when the stars inkadarat" (Q81:2), i.e., when the stars fall/scatter headlong.
A proverb: "Take what is clear and leave what is turbid."
One core meaning: hardness in a thing, from which further senses are measured.
a man who gives a little then stops giving is said to have "akdā" — likened to the digger who hits rock and must cease digging.
one sound root with three meanings
"so-and-so bought the house bi-muṣūrihā," meaning with its boundaries
He cites the poet ʿAdī: the One who made the sun a miṣr — an unmistakable boundary
one sound root whose single idea is reaching the furthest point
**majd (glory)** — reaching the utmost limit in karam (generosity, noble open-handedness).
"In every tree there is fire, but the markh and the ʿafār took the fullest share of it."
a single core idea: "coming from one place to another."
النَّبَأ (al-nabaʾ, "report, tiding") flows from the same idea
the verbs أَنْبَأَ / نَبَّأَ mean "to inform, announce."
A line of Dhū al-Rumma pictures a keen-eared creature catching a faint stir
a leaning, tilting, or deviation to one side in something
"to turn away / swerve from a thing."
A line of verse is quoted, partially, describing a cold nakbaa wind striking travelers
delay, deferral in time
the pre-Islamic Arab practice of postponing one of the sacred months to another month
a staff, so called because it is used to push/move something away (nasa'a)
Illustrated with a line of poetry describing a sturdy she-camel
is glossed here as "whatever verse We defer"
al-qafā, the back of the neck, a word he calls well known
do not judge by qiyāfa (tracking, reading traces) and conjecture
qafawtu atharahu means "I followed his track"
qaffaytuhu means "I placed him behind another"
aqnā means God gave a person that which brings ghinā (sufficiency/wealth) and that which brings qinya — i.e. stored, saved-up wealth (al-māl al-muddakhar).
what God actually gave was a qinya — a lasting possession — made up of contentment (riḍā) and obedience (ṭāʿa)
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 53:48

highlights.text: al-qistas / al-qustas -- two dialectal pronunciations of the same word -- mean "the most exact/most just of scales/balances."
the entry cites a line by the pre-Islamic poet Imru al-Qays, describing a bay-red, pure wine
the concrete image of ḥajar qāsin, "a hard stone" — the physical hardness is the origin of the moral usage
qaswa is hardness of the heart.
"then your hearts hardened" (2:74)
"the adulterated coins rang out in the hands of the money-changers"
a single root (aṣl wāḥid) whose meaning is firmness and fixity (thabāt)
al-Rass and al-Rusays are well-known valleys.
He cites Zuhayr for both, including the line "Effaced of it are al-Rass, then al-Rusays, then its ʿĀqil."
pointing to doubt, or to doubt mixed with fear
glossing rayb as "no doubt,"
rābanī hādhā al-amr — "this affair disquieted me"
"there is no rayb that there was slaughter there"
Is it over death and its vicissitude (rayb) that you grieve?
a single core idea: lightness and flimsiness/thinness
Safah = folly / light-mindedness, the opposite of ḥilm (forbearance and steadiness of mind).
cited from Dhū al-Rumma ("as swaying winds bend their tops")
swiftness of gait. Al-wajīf means speed of movement/pace.
awjaftum (the causative verb, "you made [mounts] go fast")
Al-Rāghib explains wājifah here as muḍṭaribah — agitated, quaking, throbbing
"adalla fa-ammala, wa-awjafa fa-a'jafa"
companionship. Ibn Faris treats this as a single, unified root meaning
al-khidn — "the companion" or "friend."
khidn al-jariyah — "the young woman's confidant," specifically glossed as "the one who converses with her."
